title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 23-26
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of turning inward and returning to one's original nature, rather than seeking answers or liberation through external means. This is seen as the key to awakening, and is encouraged through the study of ancient teachings, practices such as zazen, and a sense of humility and openness. By cultivating awareness and clarity in the present moment, we can embody the qualities of a Bodhisattva and radiate love and light into the world, ultimately finding liberation from our true source.

sentences.text: *Non-surpassing, non-perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million [unclear: "culprits"].
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I bow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Thank you.
I've asked people to read the poem this evening.
When it's your turn to read, will you please unmute yourself?
Chris, you're first.
*Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage.
I've built a grass hut where there's nothing of value.
After eating, I relax and enjoy a nap.
When it was completed, fresh weeds appeared.
Now it's been lived in, covered by weeds.
The person in the hut lives here calmly, not stuck to inside, outside, or in between.
In places worldly people live, he doesn't live.
Realms worldly people love, he doesn't love.
Though the hut is small, it includes the entire world.
In ten feet square, an old man illuminates forms and their nature.*
*A great vehicle bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
The middling or lowly can't help wondering, will this hut perish or not?
Perishable or not, the original master is present, not dwelling south or north, east or west.
Firmly based on steadiness, can't be surpassed.
A shining window below the green pines.
Jade palaces or vermilion towers can't compare with it.
Just sitting with head covered, all things are at rest.
Thus, this mountain monk doesn't understand at all.*
*Living here, he no longer works to get free.
Who would proudly arrange seats, trying to entice guests?
Turn around the light to shine within.
Then, just return.
The vast inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
Meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction.
Find grasses to build a hut and don't give up.
Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely.
Open your hands and walk innocent.
Thousands of words, my rigged interpretations, are only to free you from obstructions.
If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag here and now.*
Good evening, good friends, as Huy Ninh would call all of you, fellow Bodhisattvas.
I'm a little bit sad, actually.
I'm seeing the end of this poem, and it just seems to keep yielding so much for all of us.
I'm going to begin, as I have previously, with a few Shidu stories and counter dialogues.
These particularly relate to this stanza in terms of enlightenment and our ancestors.
The monk Changzhi Kuang once returned from a pilgrimage to continue his study with Master Shidu.
The master asked him, "Where have you been?"
Kuang said, "To Master Huy Ninh's memorial shrine at Taoshi."
The master said, "Did visiting there bring you any merit?"
Kuang said, "I've had some insight, but I haven't been able to open the eyes of the awakened one."
The master said, "Do you want to open the eye?"
Kuang said, "Please, master, help me do so."
The master suddenly kicked out his leg right at the monk.
Kuang had a deep realization and made prostration.
The master asked, "Why do you bow?"
Kuang said, "It's like a flake of snow landing on a red-hot furnace."
The monk Ling Mo once came to study with Master Shidu and said, "If you can give me one phrase of awakening, I will stay.
If not, I will leave."
The master ignored him.
Ling Mo shook out the sleeve of his robe and walked away.
When he got to the temple gate, the master called out, "Venerable."
Ling Mo turned his head.
The master said, "From birth to death, just this.
Why are you still searching?"
Ling Mo had a deep awakening from a talk that Shidu presented.

What I've presented, and what I'll provide you next week, is pretty much the entirety of the Shidu oeuvre, what we know of what he's written, besides the Song of the Grass Hut and the Merging of Difference and Unity.
*Our wisdom gate has been handed down from the ancient awakened ones.
Without discussing levels of mystical absorption or effort at spiritual progress, we simply actualize the direct insight that awakened mind itself is the truth.
Buddha and common people, awakening and delusion, are just different names for the same one body of experience.
You should each recognize that your own mind's aware essence is completely apart from ideas of finite or eternal.
Your nature is altogether beyond pure or defiled.
It is perfectly clear and totally complete and exactly the same in sages and in ordinary people.
It functions beyond the limits of any fixed pattern, reaches everywhere and is not contained by the labels mind, consciousness or thought.
The three realms of desire, form and formlessness, and the six states of living beings are all images coming from your own mind.
They are like the moon reflected on water.
How can there be any birth or death?
If you realize this, you have all you need.*
And following up on last week's line, "this mountain monk doesn't understand at all."
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the first ancestor, that is Bodhidharma, coming from the West?"
Shardu said, "Ask the post."
The monk said, "I don't understand."
Shardu said, "I don't understand either."
Lurie has a commentary in Dogen's *True Dharma* I, 300 koans that Dogen particularly liked.
And Lurie's comment is this:
*This question has been knocking around Zen monasteries since ancient times with hundreds of various answers.
The monastic does not understand.
The master does not understand.
Are the masters and the disciples not understanding the same or different?
If you say the same, you have missed it.
If you say different, you have missed it.
If you say neither or both, you are 10,000 miles from the truth.
What do you say?*
And the captain verse is:
*There is no place to search for the truth.
Though it's right beneath your feet, it can't be found.
Look at springtime.
When the snow is melted, the scars of the landscape are no longer hidden.*
Tonight I'm going to give you a few comments on lines 23 to 26, and we'll open up the floor to discussion and then go have breakout groups as we did last week.
*Turn around the light to shine within, then just return.
The vast inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
Meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction, buying grasses to build a hut, and don't give up.*
The first line: turn around the light to shine within, then just return.
As Ben Connolly pointed out, it has very few characters, or very few characters being very much different.
The characters in succession mean turn around, light, return and shine, which is a combined character meaning to illuminate, ease, return to, and come to.
Shurdu reminds us that it all comes from here and nothing is lacking.
The truth has never been transmitted or received.
It is not in the realm of understanding or believing.
It is the wisdom that has no teacher.
All of us are reminded to avoid running around in the midst of sound and forms and searching externally for anything.
Take the backward step and simply see that the truth has always been inherent in oneself, that is, in one's Buddha nature.
Ben Connolly reminds us that this is the most essential element of our practice: to simply come home.
We chant from Dogen's Fukan Zazengi, his universal recommendations for zazen:

*You should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.
Body and mind of themselves will drop away and your original face will be manifest.
If you want to attain suchness, you should practice suchness without delay.*

The backward step is our continuous practice, coming back to what is, so we can fully engage with a compassionate, open heart, simply to just return to the present world and to our original unconditioned nature over and over.
The vast, inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
There are previous images and pointers in the poem, the hut with the window shining and the line "the original master is present," that give us some inklings of this vast, inconceivable source.
But as Connolly points out, the Buddha never taught that there is a source.
When it says "within," it can't be faced because it is inside of us.
It's the old saying, the eye cannot see the eye.
And it can't be turned away from because it is in each of us.
Vimalakirti reminds us that we live in inconceivable liberation.
And Connolly reminds us, it's not something other than what I am doing.
I can't know it, but I'm not separate from it.
I depend upon it.
In the poem, it's the same "it" as the "it" that can't be surpassed.
Not much more to say.
The next line, meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction, is the line that really caught me when I first read this poem.
I suggested that we all secure a copy of this book, *The Roaring Stream*, because it is a great anthology of the teachings of our ancestors.
I would highly recommend that you secure a copy.
It's easy to get and it's just chock full of really great selections from our ancestors, from Bodhidharma all the way to Dogen and beyond.
An alternative reading for this line, meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction, is "engage or personally receive the patriarchs and they will come to you."
I first read this line as studying the words of the patriarchs, in terms of instruction.
But I think I've come to realize it's far more than that.
So let's investigate this a little bit further.
First of all, the word "familiar" is interesting.
Ben Connolly points out that it's related to things like family and parents and intimacy.
One of the expressions in studying Zen and our ancestors is that it's often referred to as a family business.
Zen is a family business.

It's one of the paradoxes, I think, of our practice that it both encourages this intimacy and relationship, which we think of as familiar, getting used to things, but at the same time we're always encouraged to be in a not-understanding mode, to beginner's mind.
So there's always this wonderful tension between our familiarity and our unfamiliarity at each moment.
It's interesting to me that Sher Du's historical ancestors directly were Ching Yuan and the sixth ancestor Huineng, whose funeral he was at and who he first went to practice with.
Then you roll it back all the way to Bodhidharma and the 27 Indian ancestors back to Shakyamuni Buddha that we read about in the text *The Transmission of the Lamb*.
So when Sher Du wrote this poem he had faith that others would follow the Dharma path, because the ancestors that he spoke to were the 34 or so that were before him.
And now we read Sher Du 1300 years later as one of our ancestors.
Or we say "known and unknown," as we chant about our female teachers.

With all of his intermediaries, from Yao Shan to Dong Shan to Hong Ji to Ru Jing, Dogen's teacher, and our continuing Japanese and now American lineage from Dogen to Shunryu Suzuki to now, sadly, Hakuin Sojun Mel Weitsman: these are our ancestors.
They have all gone beyond and yet they are fully present to us.
When we chant the names of the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva ancestors, the seven Dai Osho, the great teacher Buddhas before Shakyamuni Buddha, they are not historical.
They are present in our every breath.
It is an unbroken tradition connecting us intimately with all those who have gone before and those who will come after.
What a rich and complex heritage to become familiar with, to have as our family.
But they are all expressing the same root of the Buddha's teaching.
Teachings that during his apparent 80 years of mortal life were only an expedient means to instruct us in the teachings of all the Buddhas before and after him.
So how do we meet our ancestral teachers?
It seems to me we meet them in multiple ways, and let me suggest five that have occurred to me as I've been contemplating this text.
The first is from the text, when we meet and fully engage the texts that have been transmitted through space and time to us.
Everything from the Heart Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, Vimalakirti Sutra, every koan story, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
It's a huge library.
The library that Sherdu had available to him was quite small.
When I look around my room, or when we have the library at the Zendo, to see the number of texts there are, it's staggering.
It truly is inexhaustible and beyond comprehension how many words have been written about a wordless transmission.
So I would ask those of you who have the *Roaring Stream* anthology, what have you discovered in that anthology?

And for those who do not have that anthology, I would suggest that you receive a copy through Alibris or Amazon or from Henderson Books or wherever and just really thumb through and just open it up and be amazed at how deep and how wonderful and how luscious this tradition truly is.

Second, we also meet the ancestral teachers when we find out in Chapter 16 of the Lotus Sutra, the life of the Tathagata, when the Buddha tells us that he's been living in this world for an incredible, incalculable period of time, teaching the Dharma to innumerable living beings, and has also been equally in a vast number of other world spheres teaching and helping beings.

Partly what he's telling us is that our idea of the Buddha as a purely historical person who lived 2600 years ago and passed into nirvana and is no longer present with us here and now is merely a misperception.
The Buddha characterized this as a magic show that he put on, designed to capture the attention of we living beings and to guide us on the path of transformation.
The Buddha has never stopped teaching and guiding beings to liberation.
We meet him each moment.
He is always available.
Take a breath, open your eyes.
The third way I reckon we encounter our ancestors is when we sit zazen, when we are sitting as Buddhas and killing any idea of Buddha at the same time.
Dogen tells us that our ancestors have spoken highly of zazen as the Dharma gate of repose and joy.
All Buddhas and ancestors have followed this practice.
It is when and where we are most alive and aware of our Buddha nature.
A fourth way that we encounter our ancestors is when we embody the rituals of practice.

We give up our personal concerns and give ourselves up to the bowing, the prostrations, defined movements, voicings and timing that have carried our predecessors, our current Sangha mates and all future Buddhas in the Dharma.
The fifth place we encounter our ancestors is when we understand that we are each an ancestor as well.
Dogen tells us in "Buddha Ancestors" that actualizing Buddha ancestors means to uphold and see them in veneration.
It is not limited to Buddhas of the past, present and future.
But it is going beyond Buddhas who are going beyond themselves.
It is taking up those who have maintained the face and eye of Buddha ancestors, formally bowing and encountering them.
They have manifested the power of the Buddha ancestors, dwell in it and actualize it in the body.
We begin practice with an intention, whether explicit or not, to become a Buddha, to express our Buddha nature, to fully embrace our humanness.
Not through intellectual understanding but lived experience, with the understanding that our intellect enriches that experience.
In his essay The Point of Zazen, or the Acupuncture Needle of Zazen (I prefer that title), Dogen tells us that Zazen is the essential function of all the Buddhas realized in seated meditation.
Not as the way to Buddhahood but Buddhahood itself.
It is a ritualized mode of silent, persistent inquiry.
As he tells us constantly, thoroughly investigate this.
What arises?
What persists?
What disturbs?
What settles?

Our ancestors' instruction is to sit Zazen with intention and relaxation, without goals or expectations, balancing attention to form with letting go, simultaneously being present at this moment in this world with eyes, heart and hands open and receptive.
In the Buddha way, Dogen tells us, you have a human body and mind; this is a rare thing.
It's a result of endeavor in the way from olden times.
Receiving this gracious result, do not mistakenly become a student outside the way.
He relates the story of [unclear: "Shurdu"] ascending the teaching seat and saying to the assembly, our Dharma gate has been transmitted from past Buddhas.
It is not concerned with Zen meditation or effort, but it just reaches the Buddha knowledge.
We choose to immerse, entering deeply the merciful ocean of the Buddha's way, to be completely present every moment: eating, walking, sweeping the floor, reading sutras.
We recognize that the Buddha way is something that is and isn't at the same time.
It is the nature of being.
It's impermanent, and we appreciate that impermanence while we relax and practice in that joy with others.
Buying grasses to build a hut and don't give up.
Again, an alternative to the second half of that line is don't have any thoughts of backsliding.
As the poem has become instructive and directive, this is no longer the poet's voice, but he's really presenting us with our task.
We really do want to understand what our life is, and that's a continuing investigation.
I listened to a talk of Zoketsu Norman Fischer.
He had a great line.
He says, it's letting our life be our life without grasping or pushing.
This hut is now our place for and of continuing transformation and realization of the Bodhisattva path.
Don't give up.
Let's speak to persistence, diligence, faith.
Just keep showing up for morning sit, for sesshin, for your child, for your husband, for your wife, for yourself.
I've always liked the line from the I Ching, *perseverance furthers.* I think it really speaks to this don't give up: perseverance furthers.
Huineng in the Platform Sutra, the Red Pine translation, says:
*Walk the way with vigor and don't be a slacker or suddenly you'll pass your life in vain.
If you come before the Mahayana's direct teaching, press your hands together with a straightforward mind.*
And in section 43 of the sutra he says:
*Putting the Dharma into practice makes up the great vehicle.
And being versed in all teachings and skilled in all practices, avoiding nothing except the attributes of dharmas and remaining free of attachments, these make up the supreme vehicle.
The meaning of the supreme vehicle consists in the supreme practice.
It isn't something to discuss.
You have to practice it.
Don't ask me about it.*
This really speaks to our Bodhisattva intentions, to become loving, compassionate, whole people.
Self-contained, a welcoming Buddha hut with no leakage.
In zazen we encounter the expression of being a full human, a Buddha.
Our fourth vow, the Bodhisattva vow, is: Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
Just sitting zazen embodies our commitment and persistence.
And yet every moment of realization is just passing.
It arises and then disappears.
Our practice teaches us not to cling to that moment and simultaneously to trust that the next step will reveal a fresh something, never the same, as Suzuki Roshi tells us.
So we continue to yearn for the next moment of clarity, of light.
We make an effort to understand.
It's the kind of right desire the Buddha teaches, a perseverance, a focused commitment of our patience and energy paramitas.
Just sitting Buddha.
Just keep going.
The way unfolds endlessly.
It is the whole picture.
Or as [unclear: "sure do"] reminds us, what meets the eye is the way, not what we see, what meets us.
So with that I'd like to open the floor to comments, discussion about these four lines.
Hannah will ring the bell at a certain point and we'll go into breakout rooms with a question, which I'll read to you all: how does your practice and how do your readings encourage you to continue?
What is most discouraging?
So the floor is open for comments, discussion, ideas.
You have to unmute yourself when you have something to say.
**Participant:** Why do you think this translation doesn't have the stanzas?
I mean, in the way the Chinese is laid out?
Yeah.
Well, there's no separation.
We keep talking about the four stanzas, but there's no separation in the translation in the book.
**Joden Bob Rose:** No, and actually when I try to correlate the stanzas in Chinese with the English, it took me a while, because there are places where the Chinese form evidently is quatrains.
There's a classic four-line gatha, but the way that this translation was put together, for a sense of flow or whatever, broke the lines out differently.
But the classic form was quatrains.
My colleague Mr.
Hanson sees them as four lines as he reads it.
I don't quite understand how it looks that way on the page, but I think it reads across horizontally with eight lines of four pieces.
Each of those chunks of characters is one line.
They go as quatrains, as four lines.
**Participant:** Something that's standing out to me is the apparent contradiction: turn around the light to shine within and just return.
Yet the vast inconceivable source can't be faced.
So turn around and shine the light within, yet our source can't be faced.
It's a little like so many Zen koans and Dogen teachings that seem inherently self-contradicting on some level.
I think that's why I like the line from the capping phrase, there's no place to search for the truth, there's no place to find the light, and yet we know it's there.
It is the paradox of our practice, I think.
We know it shows up, but it can't be found.

**Participant:** Another thing about that line is that at the very beginning, whoever wrote the foreword, a guy named Leighton, Taigen Dan Leighton, I noted he said on page XII, that line, 23, turn around the light to shine within, then just return.
He says that contains all Buddhist practice and its primary rhythm in one line.
I put it on page XII to think about when we got to chapter 23.
And he is the translator, he, Kazuaki Tanahashi.
Oh, got it, okay.
Turn on the inner light, then just stay there.
Finding some space between thoughts, that's page 138.
I wonder what I thought was good about that.
Just finding some space between thoughts.
We shed a little light on our own consciousness.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Anyway, thank you for bringing that up.
I think Bob Penny had something on his mind.
**Participant:** I was adding to what Resula brought up about those two lines, that it also finishes out: the vast inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
It's as though we can't face it, but we can't get away from it.
I liked something on page 142, where Ben Connolly talks about just that.
And he says:
*That vast inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
The true source is vast and inconceivable.
It's beyond any ideas.
We can't turn away from it, but it's always right here.*
Maybe that fits into your question, Resula.
The mystery of those lines is grounded in the last line, bind grasses to build a hut and don't give up, which is just very banal, living day by day, moment by moment.
Taking care of the tangible, the intangible, the mystery.
That's actually all we have to do when we get lost in all the ways that we get lost in.
We just have to be here now.
**Participant:** Be here now.
A piece right before what was quoted, which is what I've been struggling not to go into:
*Where we could see connection, we see alienation.
Where we could realize humility, we try and control.
Where gratitude could flow like the rivers to the vast and rolling sea, we feel alone.
And this is why we practice.*
And I read that again today and it just hit my heart.
**Joden Bob Rose:** I know there's another hand up, and it's Valerie, and we're a little over time to go into breakout rooms.
Shuso, prioritize.
Let's hear from Valerie and then we'll go to breakout.
**Participant:** Thank you.
I'll be brief.
Just that the shining of the light is a reminder for us all to have that light shining in, to see what is our reality in this present moment.
And then when we have that, then that inner light shines out from us to help illuminate others.
And it's just a good reminder to be in the present moment and allow the light to shine within so that you have clarity and can see.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Thank you.

I'd like to also remind you as you go into the breakout room that when you come out, I'd like you to, if you want to, post a word or a couple of words in the chat to everyone and we'll read them at the end.
So thank you.
Shuso, Bob, what is your wisdom for the moment?
Unmute, please.
I guess the way to show no wisdom is not to speak.
Show wisdom.
So what we post was that in these breakout groups that people would have a comment or a word to share with everyone.
So do you have those posted, Hannah, or how do we do this?
Yeah, I do.
They're coming up.
And I will read what I have so far.
Wisdom arises, huh?
Yes, it does.
We are all interdependent beings.
Shared confusion.
We wanted to put a blank in, but we'll settle for don't know.
The unknown.
Resilience.
Paradox.
Mystery.
Both encourages and discourages.
Continuous practice.
Gratitude for hut maintenance.
Not separate.
What is this?
Accepting imperfections.
Want to put it open to the group, Bob?
Yes, please.
We could all unmute.
I could unmute everyone, actually.
Why don't you do that and then we'll trust everyone's politeness.
I guess the question is, did any of those words trigger further thoughts, realizations for those of us here on the screen this evening?

Both the practice and the place of practice and the practicer, him or herself.
That will take a long time to think through.
I said that.
You said exactly what it is.
It's all those things.
It's everything in the present.
It made me laugh.
Good.
Thank you.
**Participant:** I'm tripping over the phrase shared confusion.
Generally what is shared is agreement, not confusion.
We are confused when we share that.
It's comforting to know we're not alone in that confusion.
Oh, so much.
Thank you.
Thank you.
**Participant:** I didn't look at the Chinese in that line.
Did you, Bob?
**Joden Bob Rose:** Let me take a quick look.
It definitely talks about family.
I definitely don't understand my family.
The characters read encounter, the ancestor and teacher are a combined character, meaning a patriarch.
Relatives teach and instruct and explain.
It's definitely rooted in this notion of family relationship.
Ancestor, forefather, grandfather is the translation of the word [unclear: "ju"]. [unclear: "Chin"] is relatives and parents.
It's very much the notion of intimacy and connectivity with those ancestors.
**Participant:** I like how Ben in his book distinguishes between receiving the teachings and instead meeting the teachings, engaging with the teachings.
I really like that.
Eyebrow to eyebrow is the term in our teachings.
**Joden Bob Rose:** One on one, looking each other right in the eye.
That's why I wanted to emphasize that these are not historical figures.
These are our teachers in this moment.
They want to be our teachers and we want them to be our teachers.
It's a relationship.
Sandokai, he says, the mind of the great sage of India is intimately transmitted from west to east.
It's saying that same thing, that it's person to person.
Face to face sharing.
**Participant:** We often talk about how certain poems fall in bits and pieces in other places.
I find hints of what we read in this poem in the [unclear: "Chulmira Samadhi"] in various places.
Especially that encountering the fire, both going in and turning away, is both wrong.
That just really reminded me of what we talked about today.
**Participant:** I really like that, meeting your teachers and meeting the teachings rather than receiving them as well.
For me it was kind of timely, because I've been reading a book and was really liking what it was saying.
The teachings just seemed right up my alley.
Then I went to investigate the teacher online and find out about this.
Wow, this person really seems really great.
Then it turned out that they did all kinds of horrible things.
It was like you should never meet your heroes.
To me it was like, if you're meeting the teachings and you're able to think about them with your own critical mind, you can decide for yourself what it is you take away from them.
What part of the gift do you accept?
You don't have to put the teacher on a pedestal.
I tend to get in trouble with that over and over again.
People turn out to be human.
**Participant:** Bob, I really want to thank you for introducing us to this poem.
It's been read on so many levels.
If you think that we find what we're looking for as we read, we're all looking for different things or different levels.
As a beginner, I've found so much that's rich and encouraging.
I just love it.
Thank you.
Thank you for helping me understand it as well.
**Joden Bob Rose:** My intention was to learn as much from you as I could convey to you.
It's very much a mutual relationship here, so thank you.
Our time is coming to an end.

*Delusions are numerous.
I vow to save them.* *Delusions are inexhaustible.* *I vow to end them.* *Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.* *Buddha's way is unsurpassable.*
Thank you all.
See you at service.
Thank you, Bob.
Thank you, Hannah.
Bye.
